js_004: Who wrote “What Am I?” and what’s the book’s core idea?
js_005: A concept called “dividualism” proposed by Japanese novelist Keiichiro Hirano
js_006: A collection of treatment case studies on “dissociative identity disorder” compiled by an American clinical psychologist
js_007: A radical nihilist claim by a French philosopher that “the individual never really existed”
js_008: A neuroscience theory from a Korean brain scientist that “the self is just an illusion made by the brain”
js_009: The author of “Watashi to wa Nanika” (2012) is Japanese novelist Keiichiro Hirano. In it, he pushes back on the common belief that there’s just “one true self,” proposing the concept of dividualism.
js_011: Which is correct about the original title and publication details of “What Am I?”
js_012: Original title “私とは何か”, published in 2012 as a Kodansha Gendai Shinsho
js_013: Original title “自我論”, reissued as a revised paperback by Iwanami Shoten in 2005
js_014: Original title “心の哲学”, published in 2018 as a Chikuma Shinsho
js_015: Original title “分人の時代”, published in 2020 as a Shueisha Shinsho
js_016: The original title of this book is “Watashi to wa Nanika — Kara ‘Kojin’ e no ‘Bunjin’”, published in 2012 as a Kodansha Gendai Shinsho.
js_018: What’s the fundamental question this book opens with?
js_019: Is there really only one “true self,” the way we’ve always assumed?
js_020: Why do humans grow old and eventually face death?
js_021: Why do states try to control each individual citizen?
js_022: Can AI ever fully replace the human self?
js_023: The author opens the book by questioning the very premise we all share: that there’s only one true self.
js_025: What Western etymology does the author cite for the word “individual”?
js_026: It comes from the Latin in-dividuum, meaning “that which cannot be divided any further”
js_027: It comes from an ancient Greek word meaning “one who stands alone”
js_028: It comes from a medieval theological term meaning “a solitary being before God”
js_029: It comes from a modern French term meaning “a free citizen”
js_030: “Individual” comes from the Latin in-dividuum (that which cannot be divided). The author questions this very premise of “indivisibility.”
js_032: Which best captures the author’s coined term “dividual”?
js_033: Unlike the individual, which can’t be divided, a “dividual” is a person who can be — a person made of divisible parts
js_034: It means several people sharing a single personality
js_035: It means one person’s personality splits completely into two
js_036: It means a person who just carries out a role society assigns, without any resistance or complaint
js_037: The dividual is the author’s coined term: strip the “in-” (negation) off “individual” and fill that space with the meaning “can be divided.”
js_039: According to the author, how many dividuals exist within one person?
js_040: Not a fixed number — as many as the relationships that person has
js_041: The exact number is fixed at three from birth, determined by genetics
js_042: It grows by exactly as many goals as the person consciously sets
js_043: You’re born with one, and it necessarily splits into two once you become an adult
js_044: Dividuals exist in proportion to the number of relationships you have. Family, work, friends — each relationship gives rise to a different dividual.
js_045: How It Differs from Common Ideas
js_046: What’s the key difference between a “dividual” and what we usually call a “mask,” “persona,” or “acting a role”?
js_047: A mask implies hiding a “real face” behind it, but with a dividual, every version is genuinely you
js_048: A mask is visible, but a dividual is completely invisible
js_049: A mask can be taken off, but only one dividual exists for your entire life
js_050: Someone else puts the mask on you, but only you can decide your dividuals
js_051: Words like “mask” or “persona” assume there’s a “true self” hiding behind them. A dividual, by contrast, isn’t an act — every one of them is really you.
js_053: Concretely, how does a dividual come into being?
js_054: It builds up like a pattern inside you through repeated communication with a specific other person
js_055: Everything about it is already fully determined by genetic information from birth
js_056: It’s formed by deliberately erasing them one by one through meditation and practice
js_057: It’s officially assigned by an ID card issued by the state
js_058: A dividual is a personality formed as a pattern inside you, built up through repeated communication with another person.
js_060: How many chapters does “What Am I?” have, and what’s the topic of the final one?
js_061: 5 chapters total, with the final one covering “Beyond Division”
js_062: 3 chapters total, with the final one covering “Accepting Death”
js_063: 7 chapters total, with the final one covering “Complete Integration of the Self”
js_064: 4 chapters total, with the final one covering “The Disappearance of the Dividual”
js_065: This book has 5 chapters: Where Is the “Real Me”? → What Is a Dividual? → Seeing Yourself and Others Anew → Loving and Dying → Beyond Division.
js_067: What concern about modern human relationships led the author to write this book?
js_068: The compulsion to prove there’s one “true self” actually makes our relationships more stressful
js_069: More and more people are trying to avoid human relationships altogether
js_070: All human relationships eventually boil down to purely economic interests
js_071: Online relationships are on track to fully replace offline ones
js_072: To people confused about “which one is the real me” as they shift between different versions of themselves, the author offers this comfort: every one of them is the real you.

js_082: The English edition was published in translation by Book21.
js_083: This question runs through the entire first chapter of the book.
js_084: The Latin etymology argument is used as a core basis for building the dividual concept.
js_085: “Dividual” is the author’s coined term for a person who, unlike the “in-dividual,” can be divided.
js_086: The number of dividuals is exactly proportional to the number of relationships.
js_087: The book repeatedly emphasizes the distinction from the mask/persona concept.
js_088: Repeated communication is the key condition — a single encounter alone is unlikely to form a dividual.

js_090: The author takes issue not with relationships themselves, but with the compulsion to prove a “true self.”
js_093: A Different Face for Every Relationship
js_096: The many mes are the real me
js_103: ↻ This question will come back later
js_105: A distinct personality that forms inside you for each relationship. There are as many as you have relationships, and every one is genuinely you.
js_107: From the Latin in-dividuum, “that which cannot be divided any further” — the unchanging self-concept built by the modern West.
js_109: The proportions of your dividuals shift depending on who you’re with, and their sum total becomes your personality.
js_111: Love gets redefined as the state where the proportion of the dividual you become around a specific person naturally rises.
js_113: When you lose someone, you also lose the dividual that only existed around that person.
js_114: “Mask” or “persona” implies acting, but a dividual is different — every one of them is genuinely real.
js_115: It’s a social extension of the idea: even conflict between individuals or groups can ease if you increase the points of contact (dividuals) between them.
js_117: Some critics point out that when a relationship itself is abusive or painful, simply adjusting dividual proportions isn’t much comfort.
js_120: Everyone says they want to “find the real me,” but there may never have been just one such self to begin with.
js_121: The me at work, the me with family, the me with friends — we’re already living as several different faces.
js_122: The author says the real problem starts the moment we try to sort out which of these is “real” and which is “fake acting.”
js_123: Key idea: this book starts by dropping the premise that there’s only one “true self.”
js_126: The “individual” is a modern Western concept originally meaning “that which cannot be divided any further.”
js_127: Hirano pushes back with his coined term “dividual” — a person who can be divided.
js_128: A dividual is a personality formed as a pattern through repeated communication with another person.
js_129: Within one person there are multiple dividuals, and the sum of their proportions makes up that person’s individuality.
js_130: Key idea: a dividual isn’t a mask — it’s the fully real you, existing in proportion to your relationships.
js_133: The me around family and the me at work are different, but both are equally real, without pretense.
js_134: If a dividual from a certain relationship is a hard one, you can lower its share and raise the share of others.
js_135: Self-loathing often isn’t about hating “your whole self” — it’s really about hating one specific dividual.
js_136: The dividual that forms online is just as real as the one that exists offline.
js_137: Key idea: the way to stop hating yourself is to adjust the proportions of the dividuals that make you up.
js_140: Before it’s a feeling between two people, love is about coming to like the new self (dividual) that a relationship brings out in you.
js_141: A relationship cooling off also means the proportion of your dividual around that person is shrinking.
js_142: When you lose someone you love, alongside the grief, you also lose the dividual that only existed around them.
js_143: The author says this view connects to suicide prevention too — because one struggling dividual isn’t the whole of you.
js_144: Key idea: death and parting mean losing not just the relationship, but the version of “you” that lived inside it.
js_146: Dividualism can apply not just between individuals, but to conflict between groups and nations too.
js_147: Even between different groups, increasing points of contact (dividuals) softens the “us versus them” divide.
js_148: The urge to pin “the real me” down to one thing looks a lot like the same urge that splits others and the world into binary camps.
js_149: Accepting that you are many is the first step toward accepting that others are many too.
js_150: Key idea: dividualism is both a question about “me” and a way for the world to move past division.
js_151: That time a different you popped out and threw you off
js_152: That moment shifting between work, home, and friends, when a different version of you kept popping out, and you got confused about “which one’s the real me.”
js_153: It shows we’ve already been practicing dividualism unconsciously, all along.
js_154: A version of you that vanished after a breakup
js_155: After breaking up with someone you loved, you can no longer see that fun version of yourself that only came out around them.
js_156: It shows that heartbreak isn’t just about losing the other person — it’s also losing the dividual that was “you around them.”
js_157: Hating your whole self over one wound from one relationship
js_158: The experience of coming to reject your entire self because of a painful memory from a single relationship.
js_159: It offers a clue: lowering the share of one specific dividual can ease that self-loathing.
js_160: Around which people do I feel most like myself right now?
js_161: Increasing the share of the dividual in that relationship may be a path closer to happiness.
js_162: How much has the compulsion to pin “the real me” down to one thing worn me out?
js_163: Accepting that you contain multiple selves may actually be the path to feeling freer.
js_164: Can I accept that the one relationship (dividual) I’m struggling with doesn’t represent the whole of who I am?
